Reddit post, r/houseplants.
Title: Will it survive?

Hello everyone! I have my aglaonema for a year or so. It is getting enough sunlight I was out for a month and I make an automatic watering system for all my 50 plants and everything survived. On this plant I didn't set up correctly the amount of water and due to less water this happend. I watered it some days ago and still it is sad ! Will it survive? Should I do something?

What is wrong with my plant?
answer:
**Most likely cause: it's still too dry.** The leaves are limp but still green, smooth and whole. That's a good sign, and yes, it will very likely survive. After a month without enough water, the root ball may have shrunk away from the pot, or the mix may now repel water. When that happens, a normal watering runs down the gaps and out the bottom, and the roots stay dry. The chunky top layer in your pot makes this more likely. [Bababerry](https://bababerry.co/blogs/self-watering/how-to-rehydrate-bone-dry-soil) and [Grow Tropicals](https://growtropicals.com/blogs/houseplant-tips-tricks/how-do-i-revive-a-dried-out-houseplant) both describe this.

**Other possibilities:**
- **Roots died from the drought.** If the soil is properly moist and it's still drooping after a week, some fine roots may have died. It will perk up slowly as it grows new ones.
- **Rot from overcorrecting.** Check whether the soil stays soggy, the stems are soft or dark near the soil, or there's a sour smell. Soft, black roots mean rot. [Cafe Planta](https://cafeplanta.com/blogs/resources/aglaonema-root-rot) lists these signs.

**What to do:**
1. **Check first.** Push a finger 5 cm (2 in) into the soil and lift the pot. If it's dry or light, go to step 2. If it's wet and heavy, skip to step 4.
2. **Soak it from the bottom.** Stand the pot in 5–10 cm (2–4 in) of room-temperature water for 30–45 minutes, until the top looks damp. Then let it drain fully. If the middle is still dry the next day, soak it again.
3. **Then water normally.** Water when the top 2–5 cm (1–2 in) of soil is dry, and water until it runs out the drainage hole. Raise the drip setting on this plant's line. Keep it in bright, indirect light, out of direct sun and cold drafts, and don't fertilize until new growth appears.
4. **Leave the leaves alone and wait.** Don't cut off leaves that are droopy but green. Expect 1–2 weeks. Aglaonemas store water in thick underground stems, so they come back well. If the old stems don't stand up again, you'll see new shoots from the base. Only cut off leaves that turn yellow or crispy.
